ch1.intro: Music moves on a steady pulse. This chapter shows how fast that pulse goes, how it is grouped into bars, and why some beats feel stronger than others. Every later chapter counts in these beats.

s1.title: The beat and tempo
s1.text: The beat is the steady pulse you would tap your foot to. Tempo is how fast the beats come, counted in beats per minute (BPM). At 60 BPM there is one beat every second; at 120 BPM there are two.
s1.pulseAlt: Four seconds of beats: 4 beats at 60 BPM, 8 beats at 120 BPM
s1.words: Written music often gives the tempo as an Italian word. Each word covers a range, not one exact number, and books and composers use them a little differently:
s1.mark: Sometimes the exact tempo is written as a metronome mark: ♩ = 80 means 80 quarter-note beats per minute. The Tempo setting in Free practice works the same way.
s1.game: In the game: the count-in clicks one bar of beats at the exercise’s tempo, so you feel the pulse before the first note. In Echo mode you hear a rhythm first and tap it back without the notation.

check.question: At 120 BPM, how many beats come in one second?
check.right: Right. 120 beats in a minute of 60 seconds is 2 beats every second.
check.wrong: Not quite. BPM counts the beats in one minute, and a minute has 60 seconds.

s2.title: Bars and time signatures
s2.text: Beats are grouped into bars (also called measures). A barline closes each bar. A thin line followed by a thick one, the final barline, ends the piece. The counts under the notes show which beat each note starts on; a count in grey brackets is held through.
s2.barsAlt: Two bars of 4/4: four quarter notes counted 1 2 3 4, a barline, two half notes counted 1 (2) 3 (4), then the final barline
s2.sig: The time signature at the start says how the bars are built.
s2.top: Top number: how many beats in each bar. Here 3.
s2.bottom: Bottom number: which note gets one beat. 4 means a quarter note.
s2.twoAlt: Two bars of 2/4: two quarter notes counted 1 2, then a half note counted 1 (2)
s2.three: 3/4: three quarter-note beats per bar. The waltz is in 3/4.
s2.threeAlt: Two bars of 3/4: three quarter notes counted 1 2 3, then a half note and a quarter counted 1 (2) 3
s2.fourAlt: A bar of 4/4: four quarter notes counted 1 2 3 4
s2.common: C is common time: another way to write 4/4
s2.commonAlt: A bar in common time, written C: two quarter notes and a half note, counted 1 2 3 (4)
s2.simple: This is how 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 work, the time signatures the game uses. Some others, such as 6/8, count differently.

check.question: A C at the start of the staff stands for which time signature?
check.right: Right. C is common time, another way to write 4/4.
check.wrong: Not quite. Look at the last example of this section: C is another way to write one of these time signatures.

s3.title: Strong and weak beats
s3.text: The beats in a bar are not equal. Beat 1, the downbeat, is the strongest. Each time signature has its own pattern of strong and weak beats:
s3.middle: In 4/4, beat 3 is medium-strong: weaker than beat 1, stronger than beats 2 and 4. It marks the middle of the bar, which later chapters keep visible when they write rests, beams and ties.
s3.game: In the game: set the metronome to Beat 1 under More options, and it clicks only on the downbeat. You keep the other beats yourself.

check.question: In 4/4, which beat is medium-strong: weaker than beat 1, stronger than the rest?
check.right: Right. Beat 3 marks the middle of the bar, so it is stronger than beats 2 and 4.
check.wrong: Not quite. The medium-strong beat marks the middle of the bar.

quiz.question: How many beats does a bar of 3/4 have?
quiz.right: Right. The top number counts the beats in each bar, so 3/4 has 3. The bottom 4 says each beat is a quarter note.
quiz.wrong: Not quite. The top number counts the beats in each bar, so 3/4 has 3. The bottom 4 only says which note gets the beat: a quarter note.

ch2.intro: A note’s shape tells you how long it lasts. Start from the beat, the quarter note of chapter 1: every other value is a double or a half of the one next to it.

s1.title: Reading the shape
s1.text: Look at three things: is the note head filled or open, does it have a stem, and how many flags or beams does it have?
s1.filledText: A quarter note: one beat in 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4.
s1.openText: Longer notes. With a stem a half note (2 beats), without one a whole note (4 beats).
s1.flagsText: Each flag halves the note. One flag: an eighth (½ beat). Two: a sixteenth (¼ beat).
s1.beamsText: Flags become thick lines that join notes, one group per beat (chapter 4).
s1.staffAlt: Two bars of 4/4: two quarter notes and a half note counted 1 2 3 (4), then a whole note counted 1 (2 3 4)
s1.game: In the game: press as a note starts and hold for its whole length. A half note lasts two clicks, a whole note four.
s1.practice: Practice whole, half and quarter notes

check.question: A filled note head with a stem and two flags is…
check.right: Right. Each flag halves the note: one flag is an eighth, two flags a sixteenth.
check.wrong: Not quite. Start from the quarter note and count the flags: each one halves the note.

s2.title: The note tree
s2.text: The note tree sums it up. Each row fills one bar of 4/4, and each row has twice as many notes as the one above it:
s2.after: Every note value has a rest of the same length. Switch the tree to Rests to see them; chapter 3 explains them.

check.question: How many sixteenths fill one bar of 4/4?
check.right: Right. Each row of the tree doubles the one above: 1 whole, 2 halves, 4 quarters, 8 eighths, 16 sixteenths.
check.wrong: Not quite. Each row of the tree has twice as many notes as the row above it. Start from 4 quarters and keep doubling.

quiz.question: How many eighth notes fit in one half note?
quiz.right: Right. A half note is 2 beats, and each beat holds 2 eighths: 2 × 2 = 4.
quiz.wrong: Not quite. A half note is 2 beats, and each beat holds 2 eighths, so 4 fit.

ch3.intro: A rest is a silence that still takes up time. Every note value from chapter 2 has a rest of the same length, so you keep counting through a rest just as you count through a note.

s1.title: The five rests
s1.text: Each rest lasts exactly as long as the note of the same name. With the quarter note as the beat, as in 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4:
s1.place: The whole rest and the half rest are the same small block, so its place tells them apart. On a five-line staff the whole rest hangs down from line 4 and the half rest sits on line 3. On the one-line staff of the game, the whole rest hangs below the line and the half rest sits on it:
s1.placeAlt: Two bars of 4/4 on the one-line staff: a whole rest hanging below the line, counted (1 2 3 4), then a half rest sitting on the line, counted (1 2), and a half note counted 3 (4)
s1.count: Keep counting through every rest. Silent counts are shown in grey brackets:
s1.countAlt: A bar of 4/4: quarter on 1, quarter rest on (2), quarter on 3, quarter rest on (4); then a half rest on (1 2) and a half note on 3 (4)
s1.game: In the game: let go when a note ends and stay off through the rest. With Hold notes for their length on, as in the Learning Path from unit 4, the moment you let go is judged too.

check.question: On the one-line staff of the game, which rest hangs below the line?
check.right: Right. The whole rest hangs below the line and the half rest sits on it: their place tells them apart.
check.wrong: Not quite. Two of the rests are the same small block, and only their place tells them apart. Look again at the one-line staff above.

s2.title: Writing rests correctly
s2.text: Rests are written so that the beats of the bar stay easy to see. These four rules come up most often.
s2.silentTitle: A silent bar gets one centred whole rest
s2.silentAlt: Two bars of 3/4: a half note and a quarter counted 1 (2) 3, then an empty bar with one whole rest in the middle, counted (1 2 3)
s2.silent: When a bar is completely empty, write one whole rest in the middle of the bar, whatever the time signature. In 2/4 and 3/4 it simply means “rest for the whole bar”, not 4 beats.
s2.beat3: In 4/4 a half rest may start on beat 1 or on beat 3. Silence on beats 2 and 3 is written as two quarter rests, so the middle of the bar stays visible (chapter 1.3).
s2.writeAlt: Correct: a half rest on (1 2) and quarters on 3 and 4; then a quarter on 1, quarter rests on (2) and (3), and a quarter on 4
s2.avoidAlt: Avoid: a quarter on 1, a half rest on beats 2 and 3 that hides beat 3, and a quarter on 4
s2.dotted: A dot adds half the value to a rest, just as it does to a note (chapter 5). In 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 a dotted rest is only used when it is shorter than one beat, like a dotted eighth rest (¾ beat). A longer silence is written as separate rests that show the beats:
s2.dottedAlt: A bar of 4/4: a dotted eighth rest, a sixteenth on the a of beat 1, a quarter on 2, a quarter rest on (3), an eighth rest on (4) and an eighth on its &
s2.noTie: Rests are never tied. A tie joins two notes into one sound; silence needs no joining, and rests in a row simply add up.

check.question: In 4/4, beats 2 and 3 are silent. How do you write that?
check.right: Right. Two quarter rests keep the middle of the bar, beat 3, visible. A half rest only starts on beat 1 or beat 3.
check.wrong: Not quite. In 4/4 the middle of the bar, beat 3, has to stay visible. Which way shows where beat 3 starts?

quiz.question: A bar of 3/4 is completely silent. How do you write it?
quiz.right: Right. A completely empty bar gets one whole rest in the middle, in any time signature. In 3/4 it lasts the 3 beats of the bar.
quiz.wrong: Not quite. A completely empty bar gets one whole rest in the middle, in any time signature. In 3/4 it lasts the 3 beats of the bar.

ch4.intro: A beat can be split into smaller, equal parts. This chapter shows how eighths and sixteenths fit into one quarter-note beat, how to count them, and how beams keep the beats easy to see.

s1.title: Eighths: 1 & 2 &
s1.text: An eighth note lasts half a beat, so two eighths fill one quarter-note beat. Count the beat number on the first eighth and “&” (say “and”) on the second, exactly halfway to the next beat.
s1.staffAlt: A bar of 4/4: four eighths counted 1 & 2 &, then quarter notes on 3 and 4
s1.rest: An eighth rest fills half a beat in the same way. Count it too, silently:
s1.restAlt: A bar of 4/4: a quarter on 1, an eighth on 2 and an eighth rest on its (&), an eighth rest on (3) and an eighth on its &, a quarter on 4

check.question: Two eighths fill beat 2. How do you count them?
check.right: Right. The first eighth gets the beat number, the second the “&”, halfway to the next beat.
check.wrong: Not quite. The first eighth starts on the beat itself; the second falls exactly halfway to the next beat.

s2.title: Sixteenths: 1 e & a
s2.text: A sixteenth lasts a quarter of a beat, so four fill one beat. Count “1 e & a” (say “one ee and uh”). The number and the “&” stay where they were; “e” and “a” fall in between.
s2.gridAlt: One beat, divided: one quarter counted 1; two eighths counted 1 &; four sixteenths counted 1 e & a
s2.mixed: Eighths and sixteenths also mix inside one beat. An eighth and two sixteenths is counted “1 & a”; two sixteenths and an eighth “1 e &”.
s2.mixedAlt: One beat: an eighth and two sixteenths counted 1 & a; two sixteenths and an eighth counted 1 e &
s2.staffAlt: A bar of 4/4: four sixteenths counted 1 e & a, two eighths on 2 &, an eighth and two sixteenths counted 3 & a, a quarter on 4

check.question: An eighth and then two sixteenths fill one beat. How do you count them?
check.right: Right. The eighth lasts the first half of the beat, so the two sixteenths fall on the “&” and the “a”.
check.wrong: Not quite. The eighth lasts half the beat, as long as two sixteenths. Which count does it hold through?

s3.title: Beams show the beat
s3.text: In 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4, eighths and sixteenths are beamed one beat at a time, so you can see where every beat starts. In 4/4 there is one more rule: the middle of the bar, beat 3, must stay visible.
s3.perBeat: One beam per beat: the usual way
s3.perBeatAlt: Correct: a quarter on 1, eighths on 2 & under one beam, eighths on 3 & under another, a quarter on 4
s3.half: Four eighths on beats 1–2 or 3–4: also fine
s3.halfAlt: Also correct: four eighths on beats 1 and 2 under one beam, then quarters on 3 and 4
s3.middleAlt: Avoid: a quarter on 1, four eighths on beats 2 and 3 under one beam that hides the middle of the bar, a quarter on 4
s3.never: That last beam hides beat 3, the middle of the bar. Write it as in the first example.
s3.sixteenthsText: Beamed per beat, in groups that add up to one beat.
s3.quartersText: Never beamed: they have no flag to join.
s3.game: In the game every beam covers one beat, so each beam starts on a beat.

check.question: Which of these notes are never beamed?
check.right: Right. A beam takes the place of flags, and a quarter note has no flag to join.
check.wrong: Not quite. A beam takes the place of flags. Which of these notes has no flag?

quiz.question: In 4/4, four eighths should never share one beam over…
quiz.right: Right. A beam over beats 2 and 3 hides the middle of the bar. Beats 1–2 or 3–4 may share a beam, though one beam per beat is the usual way.
quiz.wrong: Not quite. Beats 1–2 and 3–4 may share a beam. A beam over beats 2 and 3 hides the middle of the bar, so it is never used.

ch5.intro: So far every note lasted exactly its own value. This chapter shows two ways to make a note last longer: a tie, and a dot. Ties come first, because a dot is a shortcut for a tie.

s1.title: Ties
s1.text: A curved line between two notes of the same pitch joins them into one long sound. Ties let a note last across a barline:
s1.barAlt: Two bars of 4/4: quarters on 1 2 3 4, the last one tied over the barline to a quarter on (1), then a quarter on 2 and a half note on 3 (4)
s1.middle: In 4/4 ties also keep beat 3 visible: a note that would cross the middle of the bar is written as two tied notes.
s1.middleAlt: A bar of 4/4: a quarter on 1, a quarter on 2 tied to a quarter on (3), a quarter on 4
s1.slur: A curve between two different notes is a slur, not a tie: both notes are played, smoothly connected. On the one-line rhythm staff every curve is a tie.
s1.game: In the game: press on the first note of a tie and keep holding through the second. Don’t press again on the tied note.

check.question: Two quarter notes of the same pitch are tied. What do you hear?
check.a1: Two notes, one after the other
check.right: Right. A tie joins the two notes into one sound that lasts as long as both together.
check.wrong: Not quite. A tie joins notes of the same pitch. How many times does the sound start, and how long does it last?

s2.title: Dotted notes
s2.text: A dot after a note adds half of that note’s value:
s2.tied: A quarter tied to an eighth…
s2.tiedAlt: A bar of 2/4: a quarter on 1 tied to an eighth on (2), then an eighth on &
s2.dotted: …sounds the same as a dotted quarter
s2.dottedAlt: A bar of 2/4: a dotted quarter on 1, held through (2), then an eighth on &
s2.count: So a dot works like a tie: press once and hold through the extra time. A dotted half fills a bar of 3/4. A dotted quarter and an eighth is counted “1 (2) &”: hold through beat 2 and play the eighth on its “&”.
s2.countAlt: Two bars of 4/4: a dotted half counted 1 (2 3) and a quarter on 4; then a dotted quarter on 1 (2), an eighth on &, and a half note on 3 (4)

check.question: How many beats does a dotted half note last?
check.right: Right. The dot adds half of the half note, 1 beat: 2 + 1 = 3. It fills a bar of 3/4.
check.wrong: Not quite. A dot adds half of the note’s own value. A half note lasts 2 beats; what is half of that?

s3.title: Dotted eighth and sixteenth
s3.text: The same idea inside one beat: a dotted eighth lasts ¾ of the beat and the sixteenth after it the last ¼. Count “1 (&) a”: hold through the “&”, play again on the “a”. Turned around, a sixteenth and a dotted eighth is “1 e (&)”.
s3.gridAlt: One beat, divided: two eighths counted 1 &; a dotted eighth and a sixteenth counted 1 (&) a; a sixteenth and a dotted eighth counted 1 e (&); four sixteenths counted 1 e & a
s3.staffAlt: A bar of 4/4: a dotted eighth and a sixteenth on beat 1 and again on beat 2, counted 1 (&) a 2 (&) a, then quarters on 3 and 4

check.question: A dotted eighth and a sixteenth fill one beat. On which count does the sixteenth start?
check.right: Right. The dotted eighth lasts ¾ of the beat, through the “&”, so the sixteenth comes on the “a”: 1 (&) a.
check.wrong: Not quite. The dotted eighth lasts ¾ of the beat. Count 1 e & a and find where those ¾ end.

quiz.question: Which sounds exactly the same as a dotted quarter note?
quiz.a1: A quarter tied to an eighth
quiz.a2: A quarter tied to a quarter
quiz.right: Right. The dot adds half of a quarter (an eighth), so 1 + ½ = 1½ beats, the same as a quarter tied to an eighth.
quiz.wrong: Not quite. The dot adds half of a quarter, which is an eighth: 1 + ½ = 1½ beats. That is a quarter tied to an eighth.

ch6.intro: So far most notes started on a beat. Syncopation moves the weight off the beat: a note starts between the beats, or on a weak beat, and is held through the stronger beat after it.

s1.title: Syncopation
s1.text: In syncopation a note starts on a weak beat or an “&” and is held over a stronger beat, so that beat gets no new note. The most common figure is an eighth, a quarter and an eighth:
s1.eqeAlt: A bar of 4/4: an eighth on 1, a quarter on & held through (2), an eighth on &, quarters on 3 and 4
s1.qhq: The same over a whole bar: quarter, half, quarter puts the half note on beat 2, held over beat 3. In 4/4 that half note hides the middle of the bar, so it is often written as two tied quarters. Both sound the same:
s1.qhqPlainAlt: A bar of 4/4: a quarter on 1, a half note on 2 held through (3), a quarter on 4
s1.qhqTiedAlt: A bar of 4/4: a quarter on 1, a quarter on 2 tied to a quarter on (3), a quarter on 4
s1.game: The game writes it the second way, with the tie, so beat 3 stays visible. Turn on Ties in Free practice to get syncopation.
s1.tip: In the game: press on the “&” or the weak beat and keep holding through the next beat. A count in grey brackets gets no new press.

check.question: Quarter, half, quarter in 4/4. Why is the half note often written as two tied quarters?
check.right: Right. A half note on beat 2 hides the middle of the bar. Two tied quarters sound the same and show where beat 3 starts.
check.wrong: Not quite. Both ways sound exactly the same. Think of the middle of a 4/4 bar (chapter 1.3).

quiz.question: Eighth, quarter, eighth, starting on beat 1. Where does the quarter note start?
quiz.right: Right. The first eighth lasts half a beat, so the quarter starts on the “&” and is held through beat 2. Beat 2 gets no new note: that is syncopation.
quiz.wrong: Not quite. The first eighth lasts half a beat, so the quarter starts on the “&” of beat 1 and is held through beat 2.

ch7.intro: In 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 a beat splits in two or in four. A triplet splits it in three.

s1.title: Triplets
s1.text: A triplet fits three equal notes into the time of two. Three triplet eighths take one beat, the same time as two ordinary eighths. A 3 over the group marks it, sometimes with a bracket. Count “1 trip let”.
s1.gridAlt: One beat, divided: two eighths counted 1 &; three triplet eighths counted 1 trip let
s1.staffAlt: A bar of 4/4: triplet eighths marked 3, counted 1 trip let, a quarter on 2, triplet eighths counted 3 trip let, a quarter on 4
s1.compare: Keep the beat steady: the triplet’s three notes are each a little shorter than an eighth, and the next beat comes at the same time as always.
s1.game: In the game: turn on Triplets under Extras in Free practice. Triplets are made of eighths, so keep eighth notes on too.

check.question: Three triplet eighths start on beat 1. How do you count them?
check.right: Right. Three equal notes in one beat are counted “1 trip let”.
check.wrong: Not quite. Those counts split the beat into two or four. A triplet splits it into three equal parts.

quiz.question: Three triplet eighths take the same time as…
quiz.right: Right. A triplet fits three notes into the time of two: three triplet eighths take one beat, like two eighths.
quiz.wrong: Not quite. A triplet fits three notes into the time of two: three triplet eighths take one beat, like two eighths.

meta.builds: {count, plural, one {Builds on chapter {list}} other {Builds on chapters {list}}}

tree.label: Show notes or rests
tree.bar: Each row is one bar of 4/4.
tree.alt: {count, plural, one {One {name} fills} other {# {name}s fill}} a bar of 4/4

ch8.intro: Rhythm tells you when and how long. Pitch tells you which note: the higher a note sits on the staff, the higher it sounds. The clef at the start tells you which note is where.

s1.title: The staff and two clefs
s1.text: The staff has five lines and four spaces. Notes sit on a line or in a space, and each step up is the next letter.
s1.trebleText: Its curl wraps the 2nd line: that line is G, the G above middle C.
s1.bassText: Its two dots sit around the 4th line: that line is F, the F below middle C.
s1.landmarks: Three landmark notes are worth knowing by heart: the G that the treble clef marks, the F that the bass clef marks, and middle C between them. Read any other note by stepping up or down from the nearest landmark.

check.question: Which note does the bass clef mark on the 4th line?
check.right: Right. The two dots of the bass clef sit around the 4th line: that line is F, the F below middle C.
check.wrong: Not quite. The bass clef has a second name, after the note its two dots mark.

s2.title: Treble clef
s2.linesAlt: Treble staff with notes on the five lines: {names}
s2.spacesAlt: Treble staff with notes in the four spaces: {names}
s2.aid: Memory aid: lines “Every Good Boy Does Fine”, spaces spell “FACE”.

check.question: Which note is in the lowest space of the treble staff?
check.right: Right. The treble spaces spell FACE from the bottom, so the lowest space is F.
check.wrong: Not quite. Use the memory aid for the treble spaces: they spell a word from the bottom up.

s3.title: Bass clef
s3.linesAlt: Bass staff with notes on the five lines: {names}
s3.spacesAlt: Bass staff with notes in the four spaces: {names}
s3.aid: Memory aid: lines “Good Boys Do Fine Always”, spaces “All Cows Eat Grass”.

check.question: Which note is in the lowest space of the bass staff?
check.right: Right. The bass spaces are A C E G from the bottom: “All Cows Eat Grass”.
check.wrong: Not quite. Try the memory aid for the bass spaces, read from the bottom up.

s4.title: Middle C and ledger lines
s4.text: Notes above or below the staff get short extra lines called ledger lines. Middle C sits on one ledger line: just below the treble staff, or just above the bass staff. It is the same note.
s4.trebleAlt: Middle C on one ledger line below the treble staff
s4.bassAlt: Middle C on one ledger line above the bass staff
s4.ledgerAlt: Treble staff with A3, B3 and C4 below the staff and A5, B5 and C6 above it, on ledger lines
s4.range: In Read notes, the Range setting adds the notes on one or two ledger lines.

check.question: Where is middle C on the bass staff?
check.a1: On one ledger line below it
check.a2: On one ledger line above it
check.right: Right. Middle C sits on one ledger line just above the bass staff, and just below the treble staff. It is the same note.
check.wrong: Not quite. Middle C lies between the treble staff and the bass staff. From the bass staff, which way is that?

s5.title: Two ways to name notes
s5.text: Letter names and do re mi name the same notes. Here “do” is always C (fixed do).
s5.ti: Some English-speaking teachers say “ti” instead of “si”; it is the same note.
s5.game: While you play, switch the name buttons between do re mi and letters; the game remembers your choice.

check.question: Which letter name is “sol”?
check.right: Right. do re mi fa sol is C D E F G, so sol is G.
check.wrong: Not quite. Count up from do, which is C: do re mi fa sol.

quiz.question: Which note is on the middle line of the treble staff?
quiz.right: Right. The treble lines are E G B D F, so the middle (3rd) line is B.
quiz.wrong: Not quite. The treble lines are E G B D F from the bottom, so the middle (3rd) line is B.

ch9.intro: The black keys of the piano sit between the white ones. This chapter names them: half and whole steps, the sharp, the flat and the natural, and how long a sign next to a note lasts.

s1.title: The piano octave
s1.text: An octave has 7 white keys and 5 black keys. The black keys come in groups of two and three. C is the white key just left of the group of two.
s1.pianoAlt: One piano octave: white keys C D E F G A B, and five black keys in a group of two and a group of three
s1.game: In Read notes you can answer on this piano instead of with names.

check.question: How many black keys does one octave have?
check.right: Right. 5 black keys, in a group of two and a group of three, beside the 7 white keys.
check.wrong: Not quite. Count the black keys in the octave: a group of two and a group of three.

s2.title: Half steps and whole steps
s2.text: A half step is the very next key, black or white. Between E and F, and between B and C, there is no black key, so those white keys are a half step apart. A whole step is two half steps: C to D, or E to F♯.
s2.pianoAlt: One piano octave with E and F, and B and C, marked: white keys a half step apart

check.question: Which two white keys are only a half step apart?
check.right: Right. There is no black key between E and F, so they are a half step apart. B and C are the other pair.
check.wrong: Not quite. Look for two white keys with no black key between them.

s3.title: Sharp, flat and natural
s3.point1: A sharp ♯ raises a note a half step: to the very next key on the right.
s3.point2: A flat ♭ lowers a note a half step: to the next key on the left.
s3.point3: A natural ♮ cancels a sharp or flat: the plain white key again.
s3.text: So each black key has two names: the key right of F is F♯, and also G♭. A sign can also land on a white key: E♯ is the key F, and C♭ is the key B.
s3.staffAlt: Treble staff with F sharp, then B flat

check.question: Which key on the piano is C♭?
check.right: Right. A flat lowers C a half step, to the very next key on the left. There is no black key there, so C♭ is the white key B.
check.wrong: Not quite. A flat lowers a note a half step: to the very next key on the left, black or white.

s4.title: A sign lasts for the bar
s4.text: A sign next to a note also holds for the notes after it on the same line or space, until the bar line. It only counts in that octave: an F an octave higher needs its own sign.
s4.staffAlt: Treble staff in C major with two bars: F sharp, then a plain F in the next bar
s4.after: The bar line ends the sign, so the F in the next bar is a plain F again.
s4.game: Read notes puts one note in each bar, so every sign you need is written next to its note.

check.question: A bar starts with F♯. Later in the same bar, an F on the same line has no sign. Which note is it?
check.right: Right. The sharp holds for the rest of the bar on that line, so the second F is F♯ too. The bar line ends it.
check.wrong: Not quite. A sign next to a note holds for more than that one note. How long does it last?

quiz.question: Which other name does the black key F♯ have?
quiz.right: Right. F♯ is a half step above F, and that same key is a half step below G: G♭.
quiz.wrong: Not quite. F♯ is a half step above F, and that same key is a half step below G: G♭.

ch10.intro: When a piece uses the same sharps or flats all the time, they are written once, at the start of every staff. This chapter shows how to read them and how they name the key.

s1.title: The key signature
s1.text1: The sharps or flats right after the clef are the key signature. They apply to every note on that line or space, in every octave, for the whole piece. No sign is written next to those notes.
s1.gAlt: Treble staff in G major: one sharp on the top line. A low F, a G and a high F; both Fs are F sharp
s1.text2: In G major the sharp sits on the top line, but the low F in the bottom space is F♯ too.
s1.text4: A sign next to a note wins over the key signature, but only until the next bar line:
s1.barAlt: Treble staff in G major with three bars: F sharp, then F with a natural sign, then F sharp again in the next bar

check.question: How long does a key signature hold?
check.a3: Only in the octave where it is written
check.right: Right. A key signature holds for every note on that line or space, in every octave, for the whole piece.
check.wrong: Not quite. That is how a sign next to a note works (chapter 9.4). A key signature is written once and holds much longer.

s2.title: The order of sharps and flats
s2.text3: Sharps are always added in the same order, and flats in the reverse order:
s2.sharpsAlt: Treble staff with all seven sharps: F, C, G, D, A, E, B
s2.flatsAlt: Treble staff with all seven flats: B, E, A, D, G, C, F
s2.start: Start with the keys of up to three signs: G, D and A major with sharps, F, B♭ and E♭ major with flats. Then add the rest.
s2.practice: Practice D major and B♭ major

check.question: Which flat always comes first?
check.right: Right. Flats come in the order B E A D G C F, the order of the sharps turned around, so B♭ is always first.
check.wrong: Not quite. Flats come in the order of the sharps turned around. Look again at the two staves above.

s3.title: Naming the key
s3.point1: Name the key from sharps: go one key up from the last sharp. Last sharp F♯ → G major.
s3.point2: From flats: the second-to-last flat names the key. B♭ E♭ → B♭ major. One flat is F major.
s3.practice: Practice keys up to three signs

check.question: The flats are B♭, E♭ and A♭. Which major key is it?
check.right: Right. The second-to-last flat names the key: B♭ E♭ A♭ → E♭ major.
check.wrong: Not quite. With flats it is not the last flat that names the key. Which one is it?

s4.title: Major and minor
s4.point3: Each key signature belongs to a major key and a minor key: G major and E minor share F♯. The notes read the same.
s4.game: The Key screen in Read notes shows both names for each key signature.

check.question: Which minor key shares the key signature of G major, one F♯?
check.right: Right. G major and E minor share one F♯. The notes read the same.
check.wrong: Not quite. Each key signature belongs to one major and one minor key; this section names the pair for one sharp.

quiz.question: The last sharp is C♯. Which major key is it?
quiz.right: Right. One key up from the last sharp: C♯ → D major.
quiz.wrong: Not quite. Go one key up from the last sharp: C♯ → D major.

ch11.intro: A scale is a row of notes from one note up to the same letter an octave higher, each letter once. Its pattern of whole and half steps decides how it sounds.

s1.title: The major scale
s1.text: Every major scale uses the same pattern of whole steps (W) and half steps (H), the steps from 9.2:
s1.cValue: W W H W W W H
s1.cAlt: Treble staff with the C major scale: {names}
s1.keys: A whole step skips one key, black or white: from C to D it skips C♯. A half step is the very next key: E to F and B to C have no black key between them.
s1.pianoAlt: One piano octave, C to B, with E, F, B and C marked: the two half steps between white keys
s1.white: Starting on C, the pattern lands on the white keys only. That is why C major has no sharps or flats.

check.question: Between which degrees of a major scale are the half steps?
check.right: Right. W W H W W W H: the half steps go from 3 to 4 and from 7 to 8. In C major that is E–F and B–C.
check.wrong: Not quite. Count along W W H W W W H: the 3rd and the 7th step are the half steps.

s2.title: Major scales in every key
s2.text: Start on any note and keep the same pattern. In G major the step from the 6th note, E, to the 7th must be a whole step, so F becomes F♯.
s2.gAlt: Treble staff with the G major scale: {names}
s2.letters: Each letter is used once, in order: G A B C D E F♯ G. That is why it is F♯ and never G♭.
s2.sig: The sharps or flats a scale needs are exactly its key signature (10.1): G major has one sharp, F♯.
s2.practice: Practice D major and B♭ major

check.question: How many sharps does D major need?
check.right: Right. D E F♯ G A B C♯ D: two sharps, F♯ and C♯. That is the key signature of D major.
check.wrong: Not quite. Build it from D with W W H W W W H: D E F♯ G A B C♯ D.

s3.title: The circle of fifths
s3.text: Count five letters up from C, C D E F G, and you reach G: the key with one sharp. Each step a fifth up adds one sharp, and each step a fifth down adds one flat:
s3.upTitle: A fifth up: one sharp more
s3.up: C → G → D → A → E → B → F♯ → C♯
s3.downTitle: A fifth down: one flat more
s3.pairs: Three pairs sound the same: B and C♭, F♯ and G♭, C♯ and D♭. So there are 15 key signatures for 12 different starting keys.
s3.game: The Scales hub is this circle: the major keys outside, their relative minors inside.

check.question: One step clockwise from D major: which key is it?
check.right: Right. A fifth up from D (D E F♯ G A) is A major, with three sharps.
check.wrong: Not quite. Clockwise is a fifth up: count five letters from D, both ends included.

s4.title: Minor scales
s4.text: Natural minor uses the notes of its relative major (10.4), starting on its 6th note. A minor has the notes of C major, from A to A:
s4.naturalValue: W H W W H W W
s4.naturalAlt: Treble staff with A natural minor: {names}
s4.harmonic: Harmonic minor raises the 7th note, so it leads up to the top note: G♯ in A minor. From F to G♯ is a step and a half.
s4.harmonicValue: W H W W H 1½ H
s4.harmonicAlt: Treble staff with A harmonic minor: {names}
s4.melodic: Melodic minor raises the 6th and the 7th going up, F♯ and G♯ in A minor, and comes back down as natural minor.
s4.melodicValue: W H W W W W H
s4.melodicAlt: Treble staff with A melodic minor going up: {names}
s4.practice: Practice A minor in all three forms

check.question: Which note is raised in A harmonic minor?
check.right: Right. Harmonic minor raises the 7th: G becomes G♯, a half step below A.
check.wrong: Not quite. Harmonic minor raises only the 7th note. In A minor the 7th note is G.

s5.title: Scale degrees and intervals
s5.text: Each note of a scale has a number, its degree, and a name. The names work in every key; here they are in C major.
s5.d5Text: next in importance after the tonic
s5.d7Text: a half step below the tonic
s5.intervals: An interval is the distance between two notes. Count the letters from the lower note, both ends included: C to E is a 3rd (C D E), C to G a 5th.
s5.triad: Degrees 1, 3 and 5 sounding together make the tonic triad:
s5.fixedDo: In this app do is always C (fixed do). Some teachers use movable do, where do is always the 1st note of the major scale.

check.question: In G major, which note is the dominant?
check.right: Right. The dominant is the 5th degree: G A B C D.
check.wrong: Not quite. The dominant is the 5th degree. Count five letters from G, both ends included.

quiz.question: Which step pattern is natural minor?
quiz.a1: W W H W W W H
quiz.a2: W H W W H W W
quiz.a3: W H W W W W H
quiz.right: Right. W H W W H W W: the notes of the relative major, starting on its 6th note.
quiz.wrong: Not quite. Natural minor is W H W W H W W: the notes of the relative major, starting on its 6th note.

v0_19_1.title: Fixes from a full test of the app
v0_19_1.tabs: With the app open in two tabs, one tab no longer overwrites the progress, settings or sign-in the other one saved. Your theme shows from the first moment, without a flash of the other one.
v0_19_1.pause: Pause and Resume play the paused bar again and judge it once: a tap from just before the pause no longer counts as an extra tap, a tap in the count-in no longer plays a note missed before the pause, a note tied into that bar is no longer cut short, and the count-in shows the bar it leads into.
v0_19_1.rhythm: Rhythm: every lesson's exercise has the rhythm the lesson is named after, Quit in a lesson goes back to the Path, Enter or Space on a button reached with Tab presses it instead of tapping, Skip to results adds only the time played to Minutes this week, accuracy is rounded down so 100% means every note was perfect, a perfect round's tip only asks for what can still go up, Practice weak spots always plays the rhythms that are weak, with more bars when they need them, your rhythm setup is kept after a reload, a round skipped to Results counts only the notes played on the skill map, a daily best counts only when the percentage shown goes up, a press held before beat 1 no longer runs across the timing lane, Echo shows the analog metronome, gives a listen back when the app was hidden or the sound did not play and no longer tells you to read ahead, Copy code shows the code when copying is blocked, and Play carries on silently when the browser will not start sound.
v0_19_1.staves: Staves fit their screen: every note stays in its own bar and on the staff, with busy bars drawn smaller or fewer to a row, a whole-bar rest sits in the middle, a triplet's 3, the clef, the key signature and every sign show in full, and the final barline only ends the exercise.
v0_19_1.fit: Play, Read notes and Scales fit short and mid-height phones, a phone on its side and a 1280 × 800 window, Play a 1280 × 720 laptop and a short tablet too, also with the analog metronome, ledger lines, Up & down and sixteen bars, and scores and counts stay on one line.
v0_19_1.readNotes: Read notes: after a mistake the green button shows the right name (F♯, not F), a hinted note is one to practise, a note written an octave off says so, B♯ and C♭ sound where they are written, times have a decimal comma in Dutch, C♯ and C♭ major get their key signature tip, the mi and sol lessons no longer take strict turns, a Keys lesson always has the sign it teaches, a double tap on Check no longer skips the explanation, key names stay on one line, a Hear lesson after a reload plays its notes, Needs practice lists every note, and Home's lesson preview shows the clef and key the lesson starts with.
v0_19_1.scales: Scales: Enter after a click no longer plays the same key again, Hint works after a mistake, the right note in the wrong octave says so, the circle shows each key signature whole and the progress of both spellings of a key, its keys are easier to tap, Round done names both spellings, Up & down asks for one note at a time, levels 7 to 9 name the minor keys that count, the circle keeps its key after a reload, Tab goes through the piano in pitch order, a wrong answer is read out each time, and Go round the circle no longer says the scales are shuffled.
v0_19_1.learn: Learn: a practice link keeps your own metronome, works in a new tab and gives an exercise with what the section teaches, every setup opened from a chapter keeps the way back after Start, chapter 11's Practice opens the circle with the way back, Back returns to the section you came from in one step, a phone turned on its side keeps your place, a double click on a section chip no longer answers the quick check, chapters 9 and 10 say what they build on, tables, diagrams and long chapter names fit a narrow phone, and every chapter's subtitle shows in full.
v0_19_1.accounts: Accounts: an invite or new-password link opened while someone else is signed in asks to sign them out first, Sign out with Remove waits until your progress is saved to the account, so nothing is lost or added to the wrong account, a name or email address with hidden characters is refused, a field's error clears as you type, Sign out without a connection no longer points to Keep, when you were already signed out, Sign out everywhere and Delete account say that nothing was changed, and so does Sign in; and the line that your progress is on your account shows only in the tab you signed in with.
v0_19_1.admin: Feedback and admins: a feedback report no longer keeps anything typed into a field, such as a password, or a working invite or new-password link; the feedback sheet keeps your text when your session ends; the feedback tool marks the whole button you tap, or the field of a label, names it in your language and leaves room to scroll past it; feedback, or a leaving note, of only blank characters counts as none; an account search with a hidden character works; a new link's answer scrolls into view; an account that may only invite can no longer make a new-password link for an account with more rights; a role switch changes only that role; long names and role names fit, also in confirms; and Feedback mode reaches every device.
v0_19_1.keyboard: Keyboard and screen readers: focus moves to each new screen and stays on a button that is busy or that a step replaces, or when a tablet turns, every button and example has a name, sharps, flats and triplet rests are read in words, also on Progress, Scales and the Key screen, status lines are read out, the arrow keys move through the sign choices, Escape closes every confirm and sheet, every focus ring shows in full and stands out in the light theme, high-contrast mode shows chosen options, switches, the Scales stars, the Progress charts, the Read notes and Learn bars and the Calibrate plot, and a double tap or double click on Start no longer presses a button on the next screen.
v0_19_1.misc: Smaller fixes: a skill level's check is met only by the real accuracy, so 89.5% is not 90%, text and marks with enough contrast in light and dark, Dutch plurals and wording, one minute and one check in the singular, numbers kept with their words, long emails and narrow rows that fit, 44 px targets, Calibrate and Hear it after the sound was paused, Calibrate's Save leaves no extra step for Back and its dots stay clear of the labels, practice opened from Progress goes back to it, the logo in the header is a 44 px target, a finished Path that offers no next lesson, an address the app does not have now says it is not found instead of showing a blank page, and clear messages for a name with a tab in it or a feedback text that is too long.

v0_17_1.title: Still signed in with several tabs open
v0_17_1.tabs: If you opened or reloaded several tabs of the app at once, some of them could show you as signed out, and now and then you were signed out in all of them. Now every tab stays signed in.

v0_17_0.title: Feedback on the spot
v0_17_0.feedback: For the team: an account allowed to give feedback gets a Feedback button. Mark any part of a screen and send what should change, with the screen, the spot and the device attached. Reports are saved for an admin to review in Settings → Account → Feedback.

v0_16_1.title: Still signed in after a reload
v0_16_1.signedIn: If you reloaded the app just as your sign-in renewed itself, or the connection dropped for a moment then, you could be signed out. Now you stay signed in.

v0_16_0.choice: Deleting your account now asks what happens to your progress and settings: keep them as an anonymous copy, without your name or email, or delete them too.

v0_14_0.title: Stay signed in
v0_14_0.signedIn: Once you have signed in, you stay signed in: Muzieklab keeps your session going by itself each time you use the app, for up to 90 days after you last used it. You no longer have to open your account now and then to stay signed in.
v0_14_0.safer: Your sign-in renews itself every hour, and a copied sign-in stops working as soon as it is used twice.

v0_10_0.readNotes: Read notes shows no sign buttons when no note can have a sign, its hints no longer read like the answer, and Round done shows missed notes on a small staff, in your own note names.
v0_10_0.fit: Play, Read notes and Scales now fit on a phone with the browser's toolbars showing.
v0_10_0.misc: Smaller fixes: the pad says Tap, Settings and Calibrate use plain words, the exercise code is a small Copy code button, a missed note gets a × on the staff, the “6/8 soon” chip is gone, and the Dutch app calls a path unit a “blok”.

v0_9_0.title: Read notes and Keys learning paths
v0_9_0.paths: The Path tab has two new learning paths next to Rhythm: Read notes (treble clef, bass clef, both, ledger lines, quick reading) and Keys (sharps and flats, then key signatures with up to three signs). Keys opens after Read notes unit 3.
v0_9_0.names: Tap a unit on the Path to see its lessons by name, and play any lesson you have opened.
v0_9_0.learn: A practice link in Learn brings you back to its chapter, and Read notes starts with the treble clef only; the bass clef is one tap away.
v0_9_0.scrollbar: On a computer, a page that scrolls shows a thin scrollbar, so it is clear there is more below.
v0_9_0.keys: Scales: Space and Enter press the button you moved to with Tab. Space still plays the notes again otherwise.
v0_9_0.preview: Free practice draws a new example again when you change the tempo, the metronome or the count-in, as before 0.8.0.

v0_8_0.title: Next lesson, and holding explained
v0_8_0.nextLesson: After a lesson, Results says what it opened: with two stars you see “Lesson 1.2 unlocked”, and Next lesson takes you straight there. Under two stars, Results says how many stars open the next lesson.
v0_8_0.hold: The first lesson where holding counts (usually 2.1) shows How to play again, now with holding, so the new rule never comes as a surprise.
v0_8_0.scales: Scales starts on C major: no sharps or flats, only white keys.
v0_8_0.screens: Results and the round summaries keep Retry and Next in view on short screens, and Play runs more smoothly on slower phones.
v0_8_0.notes: Read notes: a round that ended on a right answer skipped its summary and went back to the setup. It now ends on Round done.
v0_8_0.misc: The time per note no longer runs out while the app is in another tab, screen readers now read the scores in Read notes and Scales, and Reset progress also resets Free practice.

v0_7_1.title: Letters on the Scales piano
v0_7_1.letters: The Scales piano always shows A to G on its white keys, even when Read notes shows do re mi or no labels. The keyboard starts on a new key with every scale, so the letters help you find your way.

v0_7_0.title: Scales, around the circle of fifths
v0_7_0.scales: Scales: major and minor scales (natural, harmonic and melodic) in all 15 keys. Pick a key on the circle of fifths, then play the scale on the piano or spell it with ♭ ♮ ♯. A scale with mistakes comes back at the end of the round, and two stars fill its key on the circle.
v0_7_0.learn: Learn chapter 11, Scales: the major scale, every key, the circle of fifths, the three minor scales, and scale degrees and intervals.
v0_7_0.home: Home's Free practice has a third tile, Scales.

v0_6_4.title: Easier to read green text
v0_6_4.green: Green text, such as “✓ read” in Learn, Done today and your count of right answers, is a darker green in the light theme, so it is easier to read on white.

v0_6_3.title: Fairer holds
v0_6_3.lift: Holding a note is judged the way people play, not like a machine: you may let go from halfway through a note, so there is time to lift and press the next one. Before a rest the release still counts, with a little more room either side.
v0_6_3.cost: A hold that only just misses now costs a point or two instead of 20, so a run of perfect presses no longer drops to two stars over a few milliseconds.

v0_6_2.title: Desktop layout
v0_6_2.desktop: On a computer, the tabs now sit in a header across the top, and Home shows your streak, level, the daily challenge and the path beside Continue and the practice tiles.

v0_6_1.title: Language switch
v0_6_1.language: In Settings → Language, the highlight now slides to the new language, like the other choices.

v0_6_0.title: A quick check after every section
v0_6_0.checks: Every section in Learn now ends with its own quick check: one question on what the section just explained. A wrong answer tells you what to look at again, so you can try once more.
v0_6_0.read: A section is marked read when you answer its quick check right, not when you scroll past it. Sections you had already read stay read.

v0_5_0.title: A full course, from the first beat
v0_5_0.chapters: Learn now starts at the beginning: seven new chapters on rhythm, from pulse and meter, note values and rests to eighths and sixteenths, ties, dotted notes, syncopation and triplets. With chapters 8–10 on reading notes they cover everything you can practise in the game.
v0_5_0.counting: Every rhythm in Learn shows how to count it under the notes, with held and silent counts in grey brackets.
v0_5_0.practice: Each section ends with a practice link that opens Free practice set up for it, and every chapter has a quick check.

v0_4_0.title: Dutch
v0_4_0.dutch: Muzieklab speaks Dutch: every screen, the Learn chapters, coaching tips, note names and counting (“1 en 2 en”).
v0_4_0.language: Settings → Language switches between English and Nederlands. The first time, Muzieklab follows your device’s language.

v0_3_4.title: Three chapters on reading notes
v0_3_4.split: Notes on the staff is now three short chapters: 8 · Notes on the staff, 9 · Sharps, flats and naturals, and 10 · Key signatures. Sections you already read stay read.
v0_3_4.practice: Most sections end with a practice link that opens Read notes set up for that section: one clef, ledger lines, the piano, extra signs or a key.
v0_3_4.steps: New: landmark notes to read from, half and whole steps, and the rule that a sign next to a note only lasts for its own octave until the bar line.

v0_3_3.title: Learn on big screens
v0_3_3.chapter: Learn chapters use the width of a tablet or computer: a big chapter title, examples side by side, and on a computer a chapter list on the left to jump to any section.
v0_3_3.list: The Learn tab lists a chapter's sections in two columns on a tablet or computer.

v0_3_2.title: Release notes
v0_3_2.whatsNew: What's new, in Settings → About: every release and what changed in it.

v0_3_1.title: Calibrate on its side
v0_3_1.calibrate: Calibrate fits a phone held sideways: the timing plot on the left, the pad on the right.
v0_3_1.touch: A tablet held sideways keeps the wide layout, but without keyboard hints.

v0_3_0.title: Read notes
v0_3_0.readNotes: Name notes in treble and bass clef, in any of the 15 keys.
v0_3_0.answer: Answer with do re mi, letter names or a one-octave piano. On a computer, the keys work too.
v0_3_0.roundDone: Round done shows your time per note and the notes that need practice.
v0_3_0.learn: A Learn tab, starting with chapter 8: Notes on the staff.
v0_3_0.homeTiles: Free practice on Home is now two tiles: Rhythm and Read notes.

v0_2_2.title: Four-star Results
v0_2_2.stars: With a 4th star, Results shows a small arc of three stars over one big star.

v0_2_1.title: Rhythm pad on iPhone
v0_2_1.pad: The Rhythm pad no longer stops responding after iOS sends the app to the background.
v0_2_1.resume: If the sound drops out, Play pauses, and Resume starts again with fresh audio.

v0_2_0.title: Quick wins
v0_2_0.daily: Daily challenge: a new exercise every day, the same for everyone.
v0_2_0.xp: XP and levels, with a level-up sheet when you reach the next one.
v0_2_0.codes: Every exercise has a code on Results, with a Copy button.
v0_2_0.echo: Echo mode: listen, then tap the rhythm back from memory.

v0_1_0.title: First release
v0_1_0.rhythm: Rhythm practice in Tap mode: the learning path, free practice, Play and Results with coaching.
v0_1_0.calibrate: Calibrate once per device, so timing scores match what you hear.
v0_1_0.offline: Works offline and installs on your Home Screen.
v0_1_0.analog: Analog metronome: a swinging pendulum next to the beat counter.
v0_1_0.layouts: Layouts fit small phones, phone landscape and short laptop screens.
